topics.title: Subject–Verb Agreement
topics.short: A singular subject takes a singular verb (“The dog barks”); a plural subject takes a plural verb (“The dogs bark”).
topics.trouble: Learners think an -s always means more than one, so they add -s to a verb with a plural subject (“The dogs barks”). On nouns -s means plural; on present-tense verbs it goes with one.

topics.title: Agreement Past a Phrase in Between
topics.short: The verb agrees with its subject, not with a noun in a phrase that comes between them: “The box of crayons is on the shelf.”
topics.trouble: Learners make the verb agree with the nearest noun (“The list of items are long”). Cross out the phrase and read subject and verb together.

topics.title: Agreement with Compound Subjects
topics.short: Subjects joined by and usually take a plural verb. With or or nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject.
topics.trouble: Learners treat or like and (“Either the cats or the dog are hungry”). With or, look at the subject closest to the verb.

topics.title: Indefinite Pronouns and Collective Nouns
topics.short: Each, everyone and nobody take singular verbs; both and many take plural ones; some, all and most depend on the noun they refer to. In American English a collective noun like team usually takes a singular verb.
topics.trouble: Learners use a plural verb after everyone or each because the idea feels like many people. British English often treats team or family as plural; American usage mostly treats them as one unit.

topics.title: Agreement When the Subject Comes Last
topics.short: In questions and in sentences that start with there or here, find the subject after the verb: “There are two reasons.”
topics.trouble: Learners write “There’s two reasons,” as many people say in conversation. Formal writing uses there are with a plural subject.

topics.title: Pronoun–Antecedent Agreement
topics.short: A pronoun agrees in number and person with the noun it stands for (its antecedent): “The girls packed their bags.”
topics.trouble: Learners shift from one to you halfway through a sentence, or from a singular noun to a plural pronoun without noticing.

topics.title: Singular They and Generic Pronouns
topics.short: For a person whose gender is unknown or not the point, writers choose he or she, rewrite in the plural, or use singular they. Style guides differ on which they prefer.
topics.trouble: Learners are taught one choice as the only correct one. Singular they for an unknown person has been used since the 1300s; APA (7th ed.), MLA (9th ed.) and Chicago (18th ed.) accept it, AP style allows it in limited cases, and some teachers and editors still prefer a rewrite.

topics.title: Clear Pronoun Reference
topics.short: Each pronoun should point to one clear noun. “When Ana called Mia, she was upset.” Who was upset?
topics.trouble: Learners use this, it or they with nothing definite to point to (“They say it will rain.” “This shows that…”).

topics.title: Subject and Object Pronouns
topics.short: Use I, he, she, we and they as subjects; use me, him, her, us and them as objects.
topics.trouble: Learners use object pronouns as subjects when there are two people (“Me and Sam went”).

topics.title: Pronouns in Pairs
topics.short: To choose the pronoun in a pair, take out the other person: “Sam and I went” (I went); “for Sam and me” (for me); “between you and me.”
topics.trouble: Learners overcorrect and use I everywhere because it sounds polite (“between you and I,” “for Sam and I”).

topics.title: Who and Whom
topics.short: Who is a subject, like he; whom is an object, like him. Choose by the pronoun’s job in its own clause.
topics.trouble: Learners choose by the words around it rather than its job in its own clause. Many people use who for both in conversation; formal writing keeps whom for objects.

topics.title: Myself and the Other -self Words
topics.short: Use myself when I is already the subject (“I made it myself”) or for emphasis, not in place of I or me.
topics.trouble: Learners use myself to sound polite or formal (“Please send it to Sam or myself”).

topics.title: The Simple Tenses
topics.short: The simple past, present and future: I walked, I walk, I will walk.
topics.trouble: Learners think English has only three tenses. The simple tenses are the base; progressive and perfect forms add more shades of time.

topics.title: Irregular Verbs
topics.short: Many common verbs make their past forms in their own ways: go, went, gone; see, saw, seen; bring, brought, brought.
topics.trouble: Learners use the past participle as the past tense (“I seen it,” “she done it”) or add -ed (“bringed”). People say these in everyday speech; standard written English uses saw and did.

topics.title: Progressive Tenses
topics.short: A form of be plus an -ing verb shows an action in progress: I am reading, I was reading, I will be reading.
topics.trouble: Learners use the progressive for states that aren’t actions (“I am knowing the answer”).

topics.title: Perfect Tenses
topics.short: A form of have plus a past participle shows an action finished before some time: I have eaten, I had eaten, I will have eaten.
topics.trouble: Learners use the simple past where the past perfect shows which of two past events came first, or put a finished time with the present perfect (“I have seen it yesterday”).

topics.title: Keeping Tenses Consistent
topics.short: Stay in one tense unless the time really changes.
topics.trouble: Learners slide from past to present in the middle of a story, often when it gets exciting.

topics.title: Lie and Lay, Sit and Set, Rise and Raise
topics.short: Lay, set and raise take an object (you lay the book down); lie, sit and rise don’t (you lie down).
topics.trouble: Learners mix the forms because the past tense of lie is lay (“Yesterday I lay down”). Ask: is something being put somewhere?

topics.title: Active and Passive Voice
topics.short: In the active voice the subject acts (“Sam threw the ball”). In the passive voice the subject receives the action (“The ball was thrown by Sam”).
topics.trouble: Learners think any sentence with was or is is passive, or that the passive is a grammar error. It is a form of the verb, and sometimes the right choice.

topics.title: Verb Mood
topics.short: The indicative states and asks, the imperative commands, and the subjunctive states wishes and conditions that aren’t true: “If I were you…”
topics.trouble: Learners write “If I was taller” in formal writing. The subjunctive were is standard for an unreal condition there, though was is common in conversation.

topics.title: Comparing with Adjectives and Adverbs
topics.short: Use -er or more to compare two and -est or most for three or more; a few change form: good, better, best.
topics.trouble: Learners double up (“more taller,” “most fastest”), or use the superlative for two (“the tallest of the twins”).

topics.title: Adjective or Adverb?
topics.short: Good is an adjective and well is usually an adverb (“She did well”). After a linking verb, use an adjective (“I feel bad”).
topics.trouble: Learners write “did good” for “did well,” or overcorrect to “I feel badly.” Well is also an adjective for health (“I feel well”).

topics.title: Double Negatives
topics.short: Standard English uses one negative word per idea: “I don’t have any,” not “I don’t have none.”
topics.trouble: Learners miss hidden negatives like hardly and scarcely (“can’t hardly”). Many dialects use double negatives; standard written English does not.

topics.title: Misplaced Modifiers
topics.short: Put a modifier next to the word it describes. Only, just and almost go right before the word they limit.
topics.trouble: Learners leave a phrase where it lands on the wrong noun (“She served sandwiches to the children on paper plates”).

topics.title: Dangling Modifiers
topics.short: An opening phrase must describe the subject that comes right after it: “Walking home, I saw a fox,” not “Walking home, a fox appeared.”
topics.trouble: Learners assume the reader knows who was walking. The grammar says the fox was. Strunk’s 1918 rule 7 says the same.

topics.title: Commas in a Series
topics.short: Use commas between three or more items in a series. Style guides differ on the comma before the last and (the serial, or Oxford, comma).
topics.trouble: Learners are told the serial comma is simply right or wrong. Chicago, MLA and APA use it; the AP style of most newspapers usually leaves it out. Both are standard: pick one and be consistent, and use it wherever leaving it out would confuse.

topics.title: Commas in Dates, Places and Direct Address
topics.short: Use commas in dates (May 4, 2025), between a city and its state (Akron, Ohio), after yes and no, and around the name of someone you speak to (“Thanks, Sam.”).
topics.trouble: Learners leave out the comma after the year or the state in the middle of a sentence, and the comma of direct address, which can change the meaning (“Let’s eat, Grandma”).

topics.title: Commas in Compound Sentences
topics.short: Put a comma before and, but, or, so or yet when it joins two independent clauses.
topics.trouble: Learners put a comma before every and, even before a compound verb (“She ran, and jumped”).

topics.title: Commas After Openers
topics.short: Use a comma after an opening dependent clause or a long opening phrase: “When the bell rang, we left.”
topics.trouble: Learners leave the comma out after a long opener. After a short opening phrase (“In 2020 we moved”) style guides let you leave it out.

topics.title: Commas Between Adjectives
topics.short: Use a comma between coordinate adjectives (“a long, cold winter”) but not between cumulative ones (“a big red barn”).
topics.trouble: Learners put commas between every pair of adjectives. Test: if you can switch their order or put and between them, use a comma.

topics.title: Commas Around Extra Information
topics.short: Set off information the sentence could do without: “My brother, who lives in Ohio, is visiting.” Don’t set off information that identifies which one.
topics.trouble: Learners can’t tell essential from nonessential. On which and that: American usage guides prefer that for essential clauses and which, with commas, for extra ones; which in an essential clause is still standard, especially in British English.

topics.title: Semicolons
topics.short: A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses, and separates items in a list when the items already have commas.
topics.trouble: Learners use a semicolon where a colon or a comma belongs, often before a list or after a dependent clause.

topics.title: Colons
topics.short: A colon comes after a complete sentence to introduce a list, an explanation or a quotation.
topics.trouble: Learners put a colon after a verb or a preposition (“My favorites are: …”), where no complete sentence comes before it.

topics.title: Apostrophes for Possession
topics.short: Singular: the dog’s bone. Plural ending in s: the dogs’ bones. Other plurals: the children’s books.
topics.trouble: Learners use apostrophes to make plurals (“apple’s for sale”). For singular names ending in s, guides differ: Chicago and MLA write James’s; AP writes James’.

topics.title: Apostrophes in Contractions
topics.short: In a contraction the apostrophe stands for missing letters: do not → don’t, it is → it’s.
topics.trouble: Learners write it’s for the possessive. Its is like his: no apostrophe. It’s always means it is or it has.

topics.title: Quotation Marks and Dialogue
topics.short: Put a speaker’s exact words in quotation marks. In American style, periods and commas go inside the closing mark.
topics.trouble: Learners put the comma outside (“Hi”, she said), as British style often does. Question marks go inside only when the quotation itself is a question, and a new speaker starts a new paragraph.

topics.title: Titles: Italics or Quotation Marks
topics.short: Italicize the titles of long works (books, films, newspapers); put the titles of short works (poems, articles, songs, chapters) in quotation marks.
topics.trouble: Learners put book titles in quotation marks. In handwriting, underline what typing would italicize.

topics.title: Dashes, Parentheses and Ellipses
topics.short: Dashes set off a sharp break or something to stress; parentheses set off quieter extras; an ellipsis (…) marks words left out of a quotation, or a pause.
topics.trouble: Learners type a hyphen for a dash, or use dashes everywhere so that nothing stands out.

topics.title: Hyphens
topics.short: Hyphenate a compound modifier before a noun (“a well-known author”), but usually not after it (“the author is well known”), and numbers from twenty-one to ninety-nine.
topics.trouble: Learners hyphenate after an -ly adverb (“a newly-built house”), which style guides say not to do.

topics.title: Sentence Fragments
topics.short: A fragment is a piece of a sentence punctuated as a whole one: it lacks a subject, a verb, or an independent clause (“Because it rained.”).
topics.trouble: Learners write a dependent clause or an -ing phrase as a sentence (“Running for the bus.”). Writers sometimes use a fragment on purpose for effect; in school and formal writing, use complete sentences.

topics.title: Run-On Sentences
topics.short: A run-on, or fused sentence, runs two independent clauses together with no punctuation between them: “I ran I won.”
topics.trouble: Learners think a run-on means a long sentence. “I ran I won” is short and a run-on; a long sentence can be correct.

topics.title: Comma Splices
topics.short: A comma alone can’t join two independent clauses: “It rained, we stayed inside” is a comma splice.
topics.trouble: Learners join clauses with a comma and a word like however or then, which are not conjunctions (“It rained, however we played”).

topics.title: Five Ways to Fix a Run-On
topics.short: Use a period, a comma and a coordinating conjunction, a semicolon, a subordinating word, or (when the second part explains the first) a colon.
topics.trouble: Learners fix a splice by putting a comma before however. A conjunctive adverb like however needs a semicolon or a period before it.

topics.title: Parallel Lists
topics.short: Items in a list or a series take the same grammatical form: “hiking, swimming, and biking.”
topics.trouble: Learners mix forms in a list (“to hike, swimming, and a bike ride”).

topics.title: Parallel Pairs and Comparisons
topics.short: Words joined by both…and, either…or, not only…but also, and comparisons with than or as need matching forms.
topics.trouble: Learners put the first half of a pair too early (“She not only plays the piano but also the violin”).

topics.title: Capitalization Rules
topics.short: Capitalize proper nouns and proper adjectives, titles right before a name, and the names of regions, but not compass directions or titles used alone.
topics.trouble: Learners capitalize ordinary nouns for emphasis, or a family word after my (“my Uncle”), or a direction (“drive North”).

topics.title: Capitalizing Titles
topics.short: Capitalize the first and last words and the important words of a title. Style guides differ on short words in the middle.
topics.trouble: Learners capitalize every word. All the major guides lowercase articles, and/but/or, and short prepositions in the middle; on longer prepositions they differ: APA and AP capitalize words of four letters or more, Chicago (18th ed., 2024) prepositions of five letters or more, and MLA none.

topics.title: Sound-Alike Words
topics.short: Its and it’s, there, their and they’re, your and you’re, to, too and two, and then and than sound alike but mean different things.
topics.trouble: Learners trust the spell checker, which can’t tell which correctly spelled word you meant.

topics.title: Affect, Effect and Other Tricky Pairs
topics.short: Affect and effect, accept and except, fewer and less, imply and infer, lose and loose, complement and compliment.
topics.trouble: Learners mix up words that look alike. For fewer and less, careful writers use fewer with things you count; less with counts (“10 items or less”) is common and old, but many readers notice it.

topics.title: Standard Written Forms
topics.short: Write could have (not could of), supposed to, a lot, regardless and all right: the forms that formal writing expects.
topics.trouble: Learners write what they hear (could of, alot, suppose to), because in speech the two sound the same.

topics.title: Rules That Aren’t Rules
topics.short: Splitting an infinitive, ending a sentence with a preposition and starting one with And or But are not grammar errors, though some readers still object. Know the range.
topics.trouble: Learners treat old classroom bans as rules of grammar. Usage guides such as Merriam-Webster’s call these myths, while some teachers and editors still prefer to avoid them in formal writing.
